page.title: Who gets in, who gets out: the NSG rule evaluator
page.lede: Follow packets through subnet and NIC network security groups, watch rules being checked in priority order, and see why a private subnet needs a NAT gateway. Press ▶ Play to watch, or step through with Next and Back.
page.svgTitle: Network security groups deciding which packets reach Nusantara Retail's web and app servers
page.svgDesc: On the left, the internet and, later, a NAT gateway. In the middle, the virtual network vnet-nusa-shop: a web subnet where packets pass the subnet NSG nsg-web and a NIC NSG before reaching vm-web, and a private app subnet where nsg-app guards vm-app. On the right, a rule evaluator lists the rules of the NSG being checked, lowest priority number first, and shows which rule matched.

steps.title: A storefront with two tiers
steps.text: Nusantara Retail's storefront now lives in vnet-nusa-shop, 10.20.0.0/16, well clear of head office's 10.0.0.0/16. Shoppers must reach vm-web in the web subnet. vm-app in the private app subnet runs the order logic and must stay invisible from the internet. Network security groups stand between every packet and every VM, and the panel on the right shows each rule check as it happens.

steps.title: Two gates on the way in
steps.text: A network security group, or NSG, can sit on a subnet, on a network interface, or on both. Inbound traffic meets the subnet NSG first and the NIC NSG second; outbound traffic meets them in the opposite order. A packet must be allowed at every gate it meets. Here snet-web has nsg-web, and vm-web's network interface still carries an old NSG from a quick test.

steps.title: The lowest number is checked first
steps.text: Every NSG is an ordered list. Your own rules use priorities from 100 to 4096; Azure's default rules sit at 65000 and above and can't be deleted. Azure checks the list from the lowest number up, and the first rule that matches the packet decides. Nothing after it is read. nsg-web has one custom rule, Allow-HTTP-Internet at 100, then three inbound defaults.

steps.title: SSH from the internet
steps.text: A bot tries SSH, TCP port 22, against vm-web's Standard public IP, which stays closed until an NSG allows traffic. At nsg-web, rule 100 only covers port 80, and the two allow defaults only match traffic from the virtual network or Azure's health probes. DenyAllInBound at 65500 matches, so the packet is dropped at the subnet. The NIC NSG never even sees it.

steps.title: HTTP passes one gate only
steps.text: Now a shopper asks for the home page on TCP 80. At nsg-web, rule 100 matches: allowed. But the packet must also pass the NIC NSG, whose only custom rule allows SSH at priority 1000. Nothing else matches before DenyAllInBound, so the request dies one step from vm-web. Both levels must allow a packet; one forgotten NSG is enough to take the shop offline.

steps.title: One place for the rules
steps.text: Dewi deletes the leftover NIC NSG, so nsg-web becomes the single place to read and audit the web tier's rules. The next request matches rule 100 at the subnet and reaches vm-web. The reply needs no rule of its own, because NSGs are stateful. Most teams keep NSGs on subnets only; if you use both levels, always review them together.

steps.title: Groups instead of IP addresses
steps.text: vm-web's network interface belongs to the application security group asg-web. Rules can name the group instead of IP addresses, so a third web server joins the rules simply by joining the group. The app subnet's NSG, nsg-app, uses it as a source: allow asg-web to port 8080 at priority 100, then deny the rest of the virtual network at 4000.

set.t-res2: Lowest number first · first match wins

steps.title: Web calls the app tier
steps.text: vm-web calls vm-app on TCP 8080. Leaving the web subnet, the default AllowVnetOutBound lets it out. Arriving at nsg-app, rule 100 matches at once: the source is a member of asg-web and the port is 8080. The packet is delivered. The deny at 4000 and the default rules are never read for this packet.

steps.title: Same network, wrong port
steps.text: Someone on vm-web now tries SSH to vm-app. Rule 100 doesn't match, because the port is 22. Rule 4000 does: the source is inside the VirtualNetwork service tag, so the packet is denied. Without that rule, the default AllowVnetInBound at 65000 would have let it through. That's why the allow sits at a lower number than the deny it relies on.

steps.title: Calling out from a private subnet
steps.text: vm-app needs the payment provider on the internet. nsg-app's outbound defaults agree: AllowInternetOutBound at 65001 matches. Yet the packet goes nowhere. snet-app is a private subnet, the default in new virtual networks, and vm-app has no public IP, so there is no outbound path. An NSG allow is permission, not a path. The connection simply times out.

set.t-res2: the NSG allows it, but nothing routes it

steps.title: A NAT gateway opens the way
steps.text: Attach a NAT gateway with a Standard public IP to snet-app. No route tables and no changes on the VM: new outbound connections from the subnet now leave through the NAT gateway's static address, which the payment provider can add to its allow list. Replies come back, but nobody on the internet can open a connection inward through it.

set.t-res2: source becomes the NAT gateway's public IP

steps.title: What to remember
steps.text: Four habits from this demo. Plan addresses that never overlap head office. Keep rules in one place, with each allow numbered below the deny it depends on. Use service tags and application security groups instead of long IP lists. And give private subnets an explicit way out. When traffic misbehaves, IP flow verify names the rule that decided.
